done.why: I did all of the dam and the river. I drained the reservoir, raised the trunk and the trident, went down the river, dug up the scarab, and then ran myself over Aragain Falls. After I came back to life I put the trunk in the case and went back to the heaps in the Round Room. The game wouldn't let me touch them or the knee marks, so the one mystery I cared about went nowhere. The boat was gone, so I couldn't take the river again, and I left.

about: This is the old Zork house and the caves under it. The Flood Control Dam and the Frigid River have been rewritten with gentle, wry care. The reservoir is so full that it pours over the top of a dam nobody looks after. Draining it opens up the lake bed, the Atlantis room and the trip down the river. Under that runs a quieter story about someone very tidy. In the Round Room someone has sorted the cave-in rubble into graded heaps and left the marks of two knees. When you die, it seems to be the same somebody who carries your lamp back to the living room. Mostly it is about things that have been neglected, or left to wait: a dam that has never been thanked, a bubble waiting to be told it may begin, a trophy case that expects to be filled.

moments.note: The cave-ins in the Round Room: someone has sorted the rubble into neat heaps, the way some people tidy a room they never mean to use. A new and strange touch.
The five graded heaps, the swept cone of dust and the marks of two knees. A real little mystery.
I typed several moves at once, ran into the thief and got moved around more than I meant to. My own fault, but the thief showing up felt abrupt.
The dam 'has been asked to do this for a very long time and has not been thanked.' I liked it right away.
'Your load is too heavy, the sword not least of it.' Fair, and the nudge was funny, but I spent a lot of the game juggling what I carried.
With the gates open, the reservoir description still said the water 'goes over' the dam. It only caught up a few turns later.
The drained reservoir is mud with a stream 'looking sheepish.'
The trident: 'Light goes into it and comes out somewhere else. It was made for someone who expected to be obeyed by the sea.'
The room text talks about carvings and weed, but 'examine carvings' got 'You can't see any such thing.'
The boat is 'unreasonably cheerful' and 'would not care for anything sharp.' A fair, witty warning, so I left the trident on shore.
The room said a faint rumbling could be heard, but 'listen' got 'nothing out of the ordinary.'
Typing 'go upstream' near the falls killed me in a single turn, with no chance to land. The death text was lovely, though: 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.'
After I died the trunk turned up at East of Chasm, and the gunk tube was in the Gallery. It felt like someone had tidied up after me.
I couldn't examine the knee marks or pick up a pebble from the heaps. The best mystery here can only be looked at.

wished: I wanted to examine the knee marks, the dust and the separate heaps, and to follow whoever knelt there.
I wanted to examine the carvings and the weed in the Atlantis Room, which its own description mentions.
I wanted to listen at the river and hear the rumbling the room text promised.
I wanted one more chance to land before the falls after 'go upstream' failed.
I wanted a clearer sense of who the tidy somebody is. It shows up in the heaps and in the death message, and then nowhere else.

lines.line: Whoever did it knelt to do it; the dust in front of the smallest heap still has the marks of two knees in it, and nothing to say which way they went after.
lines.why: It's the most haunting sentence in the game. Quiet, exact, and it made me want to know more.

lines.line: somebody has sorted the nearest of it into neat heaps, smallest nearest, the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using.
lines.why: A sharp comparison that tells you something about a person you never meet.

lines.line: holding back the reservoir to the west with the air of something that has been asked to do this for a very long time and has not been thanked.
lines.why: It makes the dam a tired, put-upon character, and it's funny without trying too hard.

lines.line: It is dark, and has the patient look of something waiting to be told it may begin.
lines.why: Even the green bubble gets an inner life.

lines.line: Behind the dam, where the reservoir was, is a wide expanse of mud with a stream wandering across it, looking sheepish.
lines.why: 'Looking sheepish' made me laugh. It's the reward for draining the lake.

lines.line: It is deep, and would like to keep your boots.
lines.why: The mud wanting something is a nice small menace.

lines.line: Light goes into it and comes out somewhere else. It was made for someone who expected to be obeyed by the sea.
lines.why: The best description of a treasure in the game.

lines.line: weed hangs from the carvings in long, dry, disappointed strands.
lines.why: 'Disappointed' fits the theme of things left waiting.

lines.line: going downstream as if it had heard something about the end of it and wanted to see for itself.
lines.why: Funny, and also a warning about the falls I should have taken.

lines.line: anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: It ties the death message back to the tidy figure from the Round Room.

fun.why: Draining the lake and finding what it had hidden was satisfying, and so was the boat ride and digging up the scarab. The weight limit and the sudden death at the falls cost some of the fun.

engagement.why: The heaps mystery and the tidy figure kept me exploring and going back. It sagged when the mystery turned out to be something I could only look at.

difficulty.why: The puzzles were fair, and the boat clearly warns you about sharp things. The carrying limit kept me juggling items, and 'go upstream' near the falls kills you with almost no warning.

interestingness.why: The familiar dam and river feel new: neglected, a little melancholy, and watched over by someone tidy you never meet. I wanted that thread to go further than it did.

prose.why: Nearly every new description is precise and wry, and each object gets a small inner life. The few slips were the reservoir text running behind the gates (turn 69), carvings described but not examinable (85), and a rumble the room promised but 'listen' couldn't hear (104). They are small next to how well it's written.
